articleSummary: Dengue fever in children is caused by dengue virus transmitted mainly by Aedes mosquitoes. Symptoms typically appear 4–10 days after infection and include sudden high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, body aches, vomiting, and rash; most children recover in 1–2 weeks. However, the dangerous phase often occurs 3–8 days after fever starts, especially as fever subsides, with warning signs such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, nasal or gum bleeding, vomiting blood or dark stools, lethargy, rapid breathing, cold clammy skin, and reduced urination—requiring immediate hospital care. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive: fluids, rest, and physician monitoring; paracetamol for fever; avoid aspirin and ibuprofen due to bleeding risk. Aedes can be identified by white stripes on body/legs; breeding sites include standing water around homes. Prevention: weekly checks, cover and clean water containers, remove containers that collect water, and use nets/repellents. The WHO-recommended Qdenga vaccine for 4–16 years (two doses, 3 months apart) may roll out in India—consult a pediatrician.

articleSummary: As of 2026, climate change reshapes malaria transmission across sub-Saharan Africa. articleHeadline: Cảnh báo biến chứng của cúm A
articleSummary: In Hanoi, a 4-year-old girl developed acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE) associated with Influenza A after fever and respiratory symptoms. She had continuous seizures and coma within 2 days; a throat swab tested positive for Influenza A. She received high-dose immunosuppressive therapy, renal replacement therapy, and intensive neurocritical care at National Children's Hospital, but brain injury progressed and she died two days after admission. ANE is a rare post-viral brain disease, often following Influenza A, caused by an excessive inflammatory response with cytokine release that disrupts the blood-brain barrier, leading to edema, necrosis, coagulopathy and multi-organ involvement. It typically affects children 2-5 years old. No unified treatment protocol exists; early immunosuppression within 24 hours of neurological symptoms may help some cases. Influenza in children is usually mild but can cause pneumonia, myocarditis, encephalitis, respiratory failure or multi-organ injury. Parents should seek urgent care for high fever with seizures or breathing problems; vaccination is advised.

articleSummary: Bunia, Democratic Republic of the Congo — A vaccination campaign began for 50,000 frontline health workers using Merck’s Ervebo Ebola vaccine, targeting Ituri’s Bunia and Mongbwalu and extending into Nord Kivu. Ervebo was developed for the Zaire strain, but the current outbreak is Bundibugyo, for which no licensed vaccine or therapy exists; efficacy remains uncertain. The WHO authorized 70,000 doses for compassionate use in August, with 20,000 vaccinees monitored for a year. Since May, the outbreak has caused at least 3,639 deaths and about 7,541 infections, with 1,823 recoveries. Some 3,000 people have already been immunized; Bunia’s campaign doubles as field data on Ervebo’s protection against Bundibugyo. Nord Kivu cases exceed 200 weekly, while Ituri and South Kivu show variable trends. Ongoing challenges include displacement, healthcare worker strikes, and disruptions from the M23 group.

articleSummary: In the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Bundibugyo Ebola strain drives the deadliest outbreak on record. As of the outbreak’s declaration on May 15, cases have surged to 7,541 with 3,639 deaths across six northern and eastern provinces, despite weak health infrastructure and security instability. Because Bundibugyo has no approved vaccine or treatment, authorities launched mass vaccination of frontline workers in Ituri province on September 19 using Ervebo, which previously showed high protection against other Ebola strains. WHO approved 70,000 doses for DRC: about 50,000 for frontline healthcare workers and at-risk staff; 20,000 for a large clinical study on protection against Bundibugyo. Vaccines are prioritized for Bunia and Mongbwalu, with a target to vaccinate 20,000 people within six to nine months. Ituri Governor General Gaby Kasongo Mulumba underscored protecting lives. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said transmission is slowing in Ituri, and South Kivu has had no new cases since May.
